name: Ceramide EOS

lead:
Ceramide EOS (CER[EOS]) is a ceramide with a long omega-hydroxy fatty acid esterified to linoleic acid. It sits in the stratum corneum, the outer skin layer, and research regards it as essential for forming the long periodicity lipid phase of the skin barrier [5][1].
Moisturisers with ceramides aim to restore barrier lipids so skin holds water, looks smoother and feels less dry. Evidence is mostly laboratory and lipid-model work.

paras: It appears in barrier-repair creams and lotions combined with other ceramides, cholesterol and fatty acids, applied after cleansing like a regular moisturiser.
Generally well tolerated in cosmetics; individual products can irritate. Ceramide skincare is not a treatment for skin disease by itself.

chain: Less water loss from outer skin
angle.text: Ceramide-containing moisturisers aim to rebuild the lipid barrier so dry skin looks and feels smoother. CER[EOS] is one component of the ceramide mix.

lead: Ceramides are waxy lipids made of sphingosine and a fatty acid, and they form, with cholesterol and free fatty acids, the "mortar" between skin cells of the stratum corneum that limits water loss [1]. Ceramide EOS is the acylceramide of this family [2].

Studies with lipid model membranes show CER[EOS] is regarded as essential for the 130 angstrom long periodicity phase that underpins barrier properties [2]. Mouse work found that loss of Acsl1 reduced epidermal Cer[EOS] and caused severe barrier defects [3].

In disease, atopic dermatitis models show altered ceramide profiles, including EOS [4], and in psoriasis EOS is reported to fall [1]. Cosmetically, ceramides are used in moisturisers to support a smooth, hydrated barrier [5][1].
infobox: Long periodicity lipid phase of barrier [2]

paras: Ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids form the lipid matrix around skin cells, often described as bricks and mortar [1]. Neutron diffraction studies study how CER[EOS] arranges inside model matrices [2][6], and the lipid has been identified in the palate as well as skin [7].

Reconstructed epidermis models show that Th2 cytokines alter ceramide subclasses including EOS [4]. In mice, Acsl1 supports linoleic acid activation and omega-O-acylceramide synthesis needed for the barrier [3].
A 3-week study of a multifunctional moisturiser on dry legs combined biophysical measurements with visual assessment [5]; ceramides are included in many creams, shampoos and sunscreens [1].

Reviewed work is mostly lipid-model, animal and in vitro research [3][4][6][2]. A 3-week moisturiser study on dry skin assessed hydration-related measures for a multi-ingredient formula [5]; no trial isolating CER[EOS] was found.
